title: Reincarnation Research / Age of Aquarius
excerpt: Reincarnation researcher Stephen Sakellarios shared his five-decade investigation into past lives. Followed by engineer Brooks Agnew, who discussed the convergence of ancient cosmology, artificial intelligence, and global instability.
content:
About the show

In the first half, reincarnation researcher Stephen Sakellarios shared his five-decade investigation into past lives, including evidence he says links him to Matthew Franklin Whittier, a 19th-century writer he believes co-authored elements of Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol." He maintained that human beings are spiritual entities who inhabit multiple bodies in a long process of learning, moral development, and eventual "God realization." Drawing on Eastern mysticism, esoteric religious traditions, and the teachings of his guru Meher Baba, he argued that reincarnation is universal and that each life is shaped by choices made in earlier ones.

In 2005, after producing a documentary on reincarnation, Sakellarios recounted that he identified Whittier, brother of poet John Greenleaf Whittier, as a past-life identity. He explained that a colleague found Whittier's portrait: "I looked at that and it's like looking at myself... I'm looking at myself." Through his research, he claimed to have reconnected telepathically with his past-life wife, Abby, herself a writer who died in 1841 at age 24. According to Sakellarios, his research into her literary output led to a controversial discovery regarding the authorship of A Christmas Carol. He asserted that Dickens plagiarized and altered an original manuscript written by Abby and Matthew.

Sakellarios noted that Abby authored "all the spiritual elements, all of the spirits, and their talking and so on." He claimed that Dickens altered these original concepts, remarking, "those weren't ghosts. It wasn't a ghost story. It was a spiritualist story." He explained that Dickens "dumbed it down into a ghost story within six weeks to make quick cash." Reflecting on the ethical implications of this, Sakellarios observed, "I feel very defensive about what was done to Abby's work." He maintained that while the published story remains popular, "it's a shadow of what it was originally."

------------------

In the second half, engineer and author Brooks Agnew discussed the convergence of ancient cosmology, artificial intelligence, and global instability. Reflecting on his research into ancient cultures, he explained that early civilizations viewed the Earth as a living entity. "What we found was a common theme with all of these ancient cultures," Agnew said. "They actually believed the Earth itself, the planet, was a sentient being." He noted that these societies observed a direct connection between human morality and natural phenomena, stating, "We are eternal beings having a mortal experience."

Agnew framed recent technological anomalies as signs of a broader planetary transition into the Age of Aquarius, a period he characterized by individual empowerment and the breakdown of rigid centralized institutions. "Our individual force, our individual life's will, has the ability to write the future," Agnew asserted. "Yes, you know there is a creator, but we are now becoming the co-creators."

On artificial intelligence, Agnew described it as a morally neutral tool shaped by its users. "AI is stupid. It needs human guidance to be able to have purpose," he observed. "In the wrong hands, AI could be very scary, but in the right hands, we could solve everything." Asked what he would change if given the power, Agnew said he would eliminate organized religion in favor of personal spirituality. "Most of the world's wars... have been fought by bankers or churches," he claimed. "I think we can't do away with bankers, but we can certainly do away with religions."

News segment guests: John Truman Wolfe, Howard Bloom
